script.opening: "Afternoon. So the nurse said my water sample had a bit of blood in it, but here's the thing — I can't SEE any blood when I go, it looks totally normal. So surely if I can't see it, it's not much to worry about? I'd really rather not get dragged into a load of tests and hospital appointments for something I can't even see. Can we just leave it and recheck in a while?"

facts.text: If asked: the nurse dipped your urine at your blood pressure check a month ago, and again last week — "blood" both times. Nobody said anything about infection.

Never seen red or pink urine. Getting up once or twice a night for a couple of years and the stream is "a bit slower than it was". No burning or stinging when you pass water, no smelly urine, no fever, no pain in your back or side, no clots.
A bit tired since your wife died. Appetite "not what it was" but weight steady as far as you know. No night sweats, no bone pain, no cough.
If asked: smoked 20 a day from 16 until you were 51 — "gave up when my first grandchild was born".

facts.topic: Work history — only if asked about jobs
facts.text: Worked 22 years in a factory making rubber products, mixing dyes and chemicals, "in the 70s and 80s before all the masks and rules". Then a postman until retirement.
No regular tablets, no allergies, no blood thinners. Never had kidney problems. Blood pressure checked and "fine".

67, widowed four months ago — Margaret died of a heart attack. Two sons, one lives nearby. You live alone. "I've let things slide a bit since — not cooking properly, that sort of thing." Drinks "a few cans in the evening, more than I used to".

You dread hospitals since Margaret died there, and you have heard that tests mean "a camera up there" which terrifies you. Underneath: "If it's something bad, I'll be dealing with it on my own." Say these only if asked what worries you about tests, or how you are managing since Margaret died.

Polite, a bit gruff, keen to wrap up. Push for "recheck in a few months". If the doctor explains why invisible blood still matters for someone with your smoking and factory history, go quiet and then ask "What would they actually do to me?" If the camera test is explained honestly and kindly, and your being on your own is noticed, agree to the referral. If you feel lectured, dig in.

ice.ideas: "If I can't see any blood, it can't be much."
ice.concerns: Hospitals and "a camera up there". Underneath (only if asked): facing bad news on your own since Margaret died.
ice.expectations: "Can we just leave it and recheck in a while?" You will accept the tests if they are explained honestly and you feel supported.

cues: "I can't even see it." — say in the opening.
"I don't fancy any cameras." — say when tests or hospital come up.
"It's just me now." — say quietly if home life or support is mentioned.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that confirmed NON-VISIBLE (microscopic) haematuria still requires investigation and does NOT accept "if I can’t see it, it’s nothing" — it can be the sole sign of urological cancer or renal disease, even painless and invisible

Applies the NICE NG12 thresholds: clarifies dysuria and checks the white cell count to determine the suspected cancer pathway criterion (60+ with unexplained non-visible haematuria AND dysuria OR raised WCC → bladder cancer suspected cancer pathway referral), and recognises his age/smoking/occupational risk — referring on the suspected-cancer pathway where criteria are met and for urological assessment otherwise; tagged NICE NG12
Weights the RISK FACTORS (age 67, 35 pack-year smoking, aromatic-amine exposure from the rubber/dye industry) as raising bladder-cancer concern, and explains why investigation matters

Plans the appropriate work-up: confirm persistence (already repeated), exclude UTI/transient causes, check renal function and ACR/proteinuria and BP (to triage urological vs nephrological pathways), and refer accordingly (urology for cancer work-up incl. cystoscopy/imaging; nephrology if proteinuria/declining eGFR/dysmorphic picture — NICE NG203: refer if ACR is 30 mg/mmol or more with haematuria; if urology finds no cause, monitor haematuria, ACR, eGFR and BP annually while haematuria persists)

Addresses the CYSTOSCOPY fear honestly: explains what investigation involves, that it is usually quick and well-tolerated, and that finding things early is exactly the point — without dismissing the fear
Corrects the "can’t see it = nothing" misconception clearly but kindly, and surfaces the bereavement and the dread of facing tests alone, rather than accepting the deferral at face value
Supports him around the bereavement and "letting his health go", and frames investigation as worth doing for himself — engaging him rather than coercing

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges the referral/work-up (NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard: diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days of an urgent suspected cancer referral), advises to report any VISIBLE blood or new symptoms (which would escalate), confirms understanding and engagement, offers support, documents, and tracks the outcome

worked.txt: "I understand the logic — if you can’t see it, surely it’s nothing. But here’s the important bit: blood that only shows up on testing, that you can’t see, can still be the first and only sign of something that needs sorting — sometimes in the bladder or kidneys. Invisible doesn’t mean harmless. That’s exactly why we don’t just leave it."

"And a couple of things about you specifically matter. You’re 67, you smoked for a long time, and you worked in the rubber and dye trade years back — all of those raise the chance of a bladder problem being the cause. None of that means you have anything; it means you’re someone we check properly rather than wait and see."

"So let me ask — any burning or stinging when you pass water? … Depending on that and a couple of checks, you likely qualify for an urgent referral to the bladder specialists — the aim is an answer within 28 days of the referral; that’s what the NICE suspected cancer guideline, NICE NG12, sets out — and even if you don’t, you still need a urology referral. They’ll do some imaging and usually a look into the bladder. I’ll also check your kidney function and protein in the urine, because that steers whether it’s a bladder or a kidney question."

"I suspect part of the reluctance is the thought of a camera test — is that right? Let me be honest and reassuring: it’s a quick look with a fine, flexible camera, usually just a bit uncomfortable, with numbing gel, and over in minutes. People dread it far more than the reality. And the whole point is to catch anything early, when it’s most easily dealt with."

"Can I gently ask how things have been since you lost your wife? … I’m sorry. It’s so common to let your own health slide when you’re grieving, and maybe part of you didn’t want tests that might find bad news to face on your own. You wouldn’t be on your own — we’d be with you every step, whatever it showed. And doing this is you looking after yourself, which matters."

"So I’ll arrange the referral and the kidney checks. If you ever DO see blood in your urine, or get pain or fever, tell us sooner — that changes things. I’ll make sure you’re booked and I’ll follow it up with you, and we can talk again about the camera test beforehand if it helps. You came wanting to leave it; what I’m asking is that you let us check it — for something you can’t see, it’s the sensible, caring thing to do for yourself."

f.learning: Confirmed non-visible (microscopic) haematuria still requires investigation — "if I can’t see it, it’s nothing" is a misconception, as invisible, painless haematuria can be the sole sign of urological cancer (especially bladder) or significant renal disease. Apply the NICE NG12 thresholds: 60+ with unexplained non-visible haematuria AND dysuria OR a raised white cell count warrants a bladder cancer suspected cancer pathway referral; visible haematuria has its own criteria (45+, unexplained, for bladder and kidney cancer); otherwise persistent non-visible haematuria warrants urological/nephrological work-up (BAUS and Renal Association consensus 2008: urology referral for asymptomatic persistent non-visible haematuria aged 40 and over). Weight his risk factors (age, 35 pack-year smoking, aromatic-amine dye/rubber exposure), confirm persistence and exclude UTI, and check renal function/ACR/BP to triage urological vs nephrological pathways. The examinable hidden agenda is a recently-bereaved widower minimising from a mix of genuine misunderstanding, cystoscopy dread, and fear of facing bad news alone. Correct the misconception kindly, address the cystoscopy fear honestly, support him around the bereavement, frame investigation as caring for himself, and safety-net visible blood/new symptoms.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG203 (2021) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BAUS and Renal Association haematuria consensus (2008) · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023)
knowledge.summary: Persistent non-visible haematuria in a 67-year-old ex-smoker with aromatic amine exposure needs investigation, even with no visible blood and no pain. Apply the NICE NG12 criterion precisely and triage urological against renal causes.

points.h: Confirm it is real and persistent
points.t: Use reagent strips rather than microscopy. NICE NG203: persistent non-visible haematuria is 2 out of 3 positive dipsticks (1+ or more). Exclude transient causes: urinary infection (send an MSU), recent vigorous exercise, instrumentation.

NICE NG12: refer people aged 60 and over with unexplained non-visible haematuria and either dysuria or a raised white cell count on a blood test on a suspected cancer pathway for bladder cancer. Visible haematuria has its own criteria (45 and over, unexplained, for bladder and kidney cancer). Ask about dysuria and check an FBC.

points.h: When NICE NG12 is not met
points.t: Without dysuria or a raised white cell count, persistent non-visible haematuria at his age still warrants urology referral for assessment: the BAUS and Renal Association consensus advises referral for asymptomatic persistent non-visible haematuria aged 40 and over. His smoking and aromatic amine exposure strengthen the case.

Check eGFR, urine ACR and BP. NICE NG203: refer to nephrology if ACR is 30 mg/mmol or more with haematuria. If urology finds no cause, NICE NG203 advises annual monitoring of haematuria, ACR, eGFR and BP while haematuria persists.

Bladder cancer risk rises with age, smoking and occupational aromatic amine exposure (dye, rubber, leather, printing). With lower urinary tract symptoms, NICE NG12 advises considering a PSA test and digital rectal examination, after counselling.

Urology assessment usually includes imaging of the kidneys and urinary tract and a flexible cystoscopy under local anaesthetic gel. The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for a diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days of an urgent suspected cancer referral.

dg.d: Open question about his understanding of the result; let him state his wish to leave it without arguing.
Bereavement, living alone with the worry, letting his health slide, dread of hospitals, and his past work.
MSU, FBC for white cell count, U&E/eGFR, urine ACR, BP; PSA and DRE considered after counselling given LUTS.
Bladder or renal cancer, prostate, infection, stones, and glomerular disease; asked about visible blood, dysuria, fever, loin pain and weight loss.
Applied NICE NG12 precisely: 60 and over with non-visible haematuria plus dysuria or raised white cell count means a suspected cancer pathway referral.
Explained persistent non-visible haematuria needing investigation, with his age, smoking and aromatic amine exposure as risk factors.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Urology referral (urgent if NICE NG12 met), cystoscopy explained honestly with written information, nephrology if ACR 30 or more with haematuria.
Offered bereavement support and continuity; addressed his neglect of his own health; LUTS and PSA handled.
Visible blood, retention, fever or loin pain as triggers; named timescales; GP to track results and referral; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “camera up there” and “had enough of hospitals lately” and explored them to find his wife’s death.
Idea (invisible means harmless); concern (cystoscopy, bad news faced alone); expectation (leave it and recheck later).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Hospitals and "a camera up there". Underneath (only if asked): facing bad news on your own since Margaret died — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Good afternoon Mr Brennan, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for joining. I understand the nurse has spoken to you about your urine test. What have you made of it so far?
model.why: Starts with his understanding rather than the result

model.text: She said there was a bit of blood in it. But I can’t see any — it looks totally normal. So surely it’s not much? I’d rather not get dragged into a load of tests. Can we just leave it and recheck in a while?

I can hear you’d really rather not have tests, and I want to understand why. Can we talk it through — how you’ve been, what the result might mean, and then decide together what’s sensible? I won’t rush you.
model.why: Acknowledges his wish and sets a shared agenda

model.text: Fair enough.
Have you ever seen your urine red, pink or brown, even once? Any stinging or burning when you pass water?
model.why: Asks about visible haematuria and dysuria, the NICE NG12 discriminator

model.text: Never seen any colour. No stinging. Just the usual waterworks niggles you get at my age.
Tell me about the niggles. Any fever, pain in your back or side, or weight loss you haven’t tried for?
model.why: Characterises LUTS and screens for infection, stones and systemic features

model.text: Nothing like that. Just the niggles.
I see from your notes you used to smoke, and you worked in the rubber and dye trade. Can you tell me about that work?
model.why: Explores the occupational and smoking risk factors

model.text: Years back. Smoked a long time too, gave up. Why’s that matter?
Some chemicals used in that work, and long-term smoking, both make bladder problems more likely. It doesn’t mean you have anything — it means we check properly rather than wait and see.
model.why: Explains why his risk factors matter without alarming

model.text: Nobody ever told me that.
You said you’d rather not be dragged into tests. What is it about the tests that puts you off?
model.why: Follows the reluctance cue to its source

model.text: They’ll want a camera up there, won’t they? I’ve heard about that. And hospitals… I’ve had enough of hospitals lately.
Lately?
model.why: Reflects the cue and gives space

model.text: (Pause.) My wife. She died. I’ve not really looked after myself since. And if they find something… there’s no one to go through it with.

I’m so sorry. That’s a huge loss, and it’s very common to let your own health slide while grieving. It makes sense that tests which might bring bad news feel like too much on your own. Thank you for telling me.
model.why: Responds to the bereavement and names the fear underneath

model.text: Let me be honest about the result. Blood you can’t see, that only shows on testing, can still be the first sign of something in the bladder or kidneys that needs sorting. Often the cause is harmless, like the prostate. But at 67, with your smoking and that work, it needs checking properly rather than leaving.
model.why: Corrects the misconception with honest, proportionate risk

model.text: So invisible doesn’t mean harmless.

Exactly. I’d like some tests first: a urine sample for infection, a blood count and kidney test, a urine protein test, and a blood pressure check. I’d also suggest a prostate blood test, given the waterworks niggles, and I’ll explain the pros and cons of that. Then a referral to the urology specialists — urgent if the blood count shows raised white cells.
model.why: Work-up per NICE NG12 and NG203 with PSA counselling and referral route

model.text: And the camera?

They’ll usually scan your kidneys and have a look in the bladder with a thin, bendy camera. It’s done with numbing gel, takes a few minutes, and you go home the same day. Most people say the dread was worse than the test. Would it help if I sent you some written information about it?
model.why: Explains cystoscopy honestly and offers information

model.text: It would. I’d rather know what I’m walking into.

And you won’t be on your own with this. I’ll ring you with every result and before the appointment if you want. Would you also like details of bereavement support? Many people find it helps, whenever they’re ready.
model.why: Offers continuity and bereavement support as part of the plan

model.text: Maybe. I’ll think about it. Alright — let’s do the tests.
Thank you. The practice will book the blood tests this week and I’ll send the referral as soon as the results are back. If it’s the urgent route, the aim is for an answer within four weeks.
model.why: Specific timescales and ownership of the next steps

model.text: If you ever see blood in your urine, can’t pass water, or get a fever or pain in your side, contact us the same day — that changes things. Otherwise I’ll be in touch with the results.
Right you are.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well, what will you do next, and why?
model.why: Teach-back to confirm understanding and engagement

model.text: Bloods and a sample this week, then the bladder specialists. Because not seeing blood doesn’t mean it’s nothing, especially with my smoking and the old job.
That’s it. Coming today was you looking after yourself, and that matters. I’ll speak to you soon.
model.why: Warm close that frames investigation as self-care

social.t: Recently widowed and neglecting his health, he dreads facing bad news alone. Continuity with one GP and a clear plan make engagement likelier.
Past work in the rubber and dye industry involved aromatic amines, a recognised bladder cancer risk. Many patients never connect old jobs to present risk.

legal.t: If bladder cancer were diagnosed, cancer of the urinary tract after aromatic amine exposure can be a prescribed disease under the Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit scheme. Record the occupational history now; raise it only if relevant.

professional.t: He may still decline. Explain the specific risks of not investigating, check he understands, record his decision and keep the offer open (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).
Track the MSU, FBC and referral to completion; a suspected cancer referral needs a practice system to confirm the appointment happens.

community.t: Cruse Bereavement Support; Fight Bladder Cancer and Macmillan for information if needed; Prostate Cancer UK for balanced PSA information.

redFlags: Visible haematuria at any point — NICE NG12 criteria for 45 and over
Dysuria or raised white cell count with non-visible haematuria at 60 and over — suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12)
Weight loss, loin pain, fever or urinary retention
psychosocial: Recently widowed and letting his health slide
Dread of hospitals and specifically of cystoscopy
Fear of facing bad news alone
ice: Idea: if he can’t see blood, it can’t be significant
Concern: a “camera up there”; bad news with no one to share it
Expectation: leave it and recheck later

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest: “Your urine has had blood in it twice that you can’t see. Often there’s a harmless cause, but at 67 with your smoking and your old job, it needs proper checking — invisible doesn’t mean harmless.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s like a warning light on a car dashboard. The car still drives fine and you can’t see anything wrong, but the light means a mechanic should have a look. Most of the time it’s something small — but you don’t ignore the light.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been through so much since your wife died, and the thought of tests with bad news at the end, on your own, is a lot. You won’t be on your own — I’ll be with you at each step.”
management.psychosocial: Build continuity into the plan: the same GP phones with results, written information about cystoscopy, and an offer of bereavement support.
sharedPlan: MSU, FBC, U&E/eGFR, urine ACR, BP; PSA and DRE after counselling (LUTS)
Urology referral: suspected cancer pathway if dysuria or raised white cell count (NICE NG12); otherwise routine urology for persistent non-visible haematuria at 40 and over
Nephrology if ACR 30 or more with haematuria (NICE NG203)
safetyNet: Same-day contact for visible blood, retention, fever or loin pain
GP tracks results and referral; phone follow-up with results

pitfalls.intro: Candidates lose this station by accepting his logic that invisible means harmless, by quoting the wrong NICE NG12 threshold, or by pushing tests on a grieving man without finding out why he is reluctant.

items.fail: Agreeing to recheck the urine in three months.
items.why: Persistent non-visible haematuria is already confirmed; delay in a high-risk man is unsafe management.
items.fix: “It’s been confirmed twice. At your age and with your history, we check it properly now.”

items.fail: Quoting the visible haematuria criterion, or referring urgently without checking the white cell count.
items.why: NICE NG12 for non-visible haematuria requires age 60 and over plus dysuria or a raised white cell count. Precision is marked.
items.fix: Ask about dysuria and send an FBC; route the referral by the result.

items.fail: Never asking about occupation or smoking.
items.why: Aromatic amine exposure and 35 pack-years are central to his risk and to persuading him.
items.fix: Ask about past work and smoking and explain why they matter.

items.fail: Pressing on with the plan when he says “I’ve had enough of hospitals lately”.
items.why: “Does not respond to cues.” The bereavement is why he is avoiding tests.
items.fix: Reflect it back — “Lately?” — and give him space.

items.fail: Telling him cystoscopy is nothing to worry about.
items.why: Dismissing a specific fear rarely removes it.
items.fix: Describe it concretely and offer written information.

items.fail: Promising he will be seen within two weeks.
items.why: The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard is a diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days; a two-week promise is outdated.
items.fix: “On the urgent route, the aim is an answer within four weeks.”

timeMap.d: Ask what he has made of the result. He wants to leave it. Acknowledge that and agree to decide together.
Visible blood, dysuria, LUTS, fever, loin pain, weight loss; smoking and the rubber and dye work.
The camera fear and “enough of hospitals last year” lead to his wife’s death and fear of facing bad news alone.
Invisible is not harmless. MSU, FBC, eGFR, ACR, BP, PSA with counselling. Urology referral, urgent if NICE NG12 is met. Cystoscopy explained honestly.
Same-day triggers, timescales, GP continuity, bereavement support offered. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Agrees to recheck in a few months; never asks about dysuria or occupation; no FBC; dismisses the cystoscopy fear or doesn’t find it; misses the bereavement entirely.
wordPics.pass: Explains that non-visible haematuria needs investigation; asks about dysuria and risk factors; arranges MSU, bloods and urology referral; basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: applies the NICE NG12 criterion precisely with an FBC; names his occupational and smoking risk; counsels on PSA; explains cystoscopy honestly; finds the bereavement and offers continuity and support; teach-back and clear timescales.

avoid.dont: “It’s only microscopic, so it’s probably nothing.”
avoid.instead: “Blood you can’t see can still be the first sign of something that needs sorting, so we check it properly.”
avoid.why: Endorsing his misconception is the central clinical fail.

avoid.dont: “Cystoscopy is a routine procedure, there’s nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “It’s a thin, bendy camera with numbing gel, a few minutes, and home the same day. Most people say the dread was worse.”
avoid.why: Dismissing a fear keeps it alive; a concrete description reduces it.

I’d also suggest a prostate blood test, given the waterworks niggles, and I’ll explain the pros and cons of that. Then a referral to the urology specialists — urgent if the blood count shows raised white cells.
SCA_MODELS.why: Work-up per NICE NG12 and NG203 with PSA counselling and referral route

SCA_MODELS.text: And the camera?

They’ll usually scan your kidneys and have a look in the bladder with a thin, bendy camera. It’s done with numbing gel, takes a few minutes, and you go home the same day. Most people say the dread was worse than the test. Would it help if I sent you some written information about it?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains cystoscopy honestly and offers information

SCA_MODELS.text: It would. I’d rather know what I’m walking into.

And you won’t be on your own with this. I’ll ring you with every result and before the appointment if you want. Would you also like details of bereavement support? Many people find it helps, whenever they’re ready.
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers continuity and bereavement support as part of the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. I’ll think about it. Alright — let’s do the tests.
Thank you. The practice will book the blood tests this week and I’ll send the referral as soon as the results are back. If it’s the urgent route, the aim is for an answer within four weeks.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific timescales and ownership of the next steps

SCA_MODELS.text: If you ever see blood in your urine, can’t pass water, or get a fever or pain in your side, contact us the same day — that changes things. Otherwise I’ll be in touch with the results.
Right you are.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well, what will you do next, and why?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back to confirm understanding and engagement

SCA_MODELS.text: Bloods and a sample this week, then the bladder specialists. Because not seeing blood doesn’t mean it’s nothing, especially with my smoking and the old job.
That’s it. Coming today was you looking after yourself, and that matters. I’ll speak to you soon.
SCA_MODELS.why: Warm close that frames investigation as self-care

SCA_STEM.name: Alec Brennan
pmh: Previous occupational exposure: rubber and dye industry
SCA_STEM.recent: Urine dipstick done for an unrelated reason showed blood; confirmed on repeat dipstick. No proteinuria. BP normal. eGFR normal. No visible haematuria reported.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss the urine result. Nurse note: “reluctant to have tests”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG203 (2021) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BAUS and Renal Association haematuria consensus (2008) · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Persistent non-visible haematuria in a 67-year-old ex-smoker with aromatic amine exposure needs investigation, even with no visible blood and no pain. Apply the NICE NG12 criterion precisely and triage urological against renal causes.

points.h: Confirm it is real and persistent
points.t: Use reagent strips rather than microscopy. NICE NG203: persistent non-visible haematuria is 2 out of 3 positive dipsticks (1+ or more). Exclude transient causes: urinary infection (send an MSU), recent vigorous exercise, instrumentation.

NICE NG12: refer people aged 60 and over with unexplained non-visible haematuria and either dysuria or a raised white cell count on a blood test on a suspected cancer pathway for bladder cancer. Visible haematuria has its own criteria (45 and over, unexplained, for bladder and kidney cancer). Ask about dysuria and check an FBC.

points.h: When NICE NG12 is not met
points.t: Without dysuria or a raised white cell count, persistent non-visible haematuria at his age still warrants urology referral for assessment: the BAUS and Renal Association consensus advises referral for asymptomatic persistent non-visible haematuria aged 40 and over. His smoking and aromatic amine exposure strengthen the case.

Check eGFR, urine ACR and BP. NICE NG203: refer to nephrology if ACR is 30 mg/mmol or more with haematuria. If urology finds no cause, NICE NG203 advises annual monitoring of haematuria, ACR, eGFR and BP while haematuria persists.

Bladder cancer risk rises with age, smoking and occupational aromatic amine exposure (dye, rubber, leather, printing). With lower urinary tract symptoms, NICE NG12 advises considering a PSA test and digital rectal examination, after counselling.

Urology assessment usually includes imaging of the kidneys and urinary tract and a flexible cystoscopy under local anaesthetic gel. The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for a diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days of an urgent suspected cancer referral.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question about his understanding of the result; let him state his wish to leave it without arguing.
Bereavement, living alone with the worry, letting his health slide, dread of hospitals, and his past work.
Picked up “camera up there” and “had enough of hospitals lately” and explored them to find his wife’s death.
Idea (invisible means harmless); concern (cystoscopy, bad news faced alone); expectation (leave it and recheck later).
MSU, FBC for white cell count, U&E/eGFR, urine ACR, BP; PSA and DRE considered after counselling given LUTS.
Bladder or renal cancer, prostate, infection, stones, and glomerular disease; asked about visible blood, dysuria, fever, loin pain and weight loss.
Applied NICE NG12 precisely: 60 and over with non-visible haematuria plus dysuria or raised white cell count means a suspected cancer pathway referral.
Explained persistent non-visible haematuria needing investigation, with his age, smoking and aromatic amine exposure as risk factors.
Urology referral (urgent if NICE NG12 met), cystoscopy explained honestly with written information, nephrology if ACR 30 or more with haematuria.
Offered bereavement support and continuity; addressed his neglect of his own health; LUTS and PSA handled.
Visible blood, retention, fever or loin pain as triggers; named timescales; GP to track results and referral; teach-back.

social.t: Recently widowed and neglecting his health, he dreads facing bad news alone. Continuity with one GP and a clear plan make engagement likelier.
Past work in the rubber and dye industry involved aromatic amines, a recognised bladder cancer risk. Many patients never connect old jobs to present risk.

legal.t: If bladder cancer were diagnosed, cancer of the urinary tract after aromatic amine exposure can be a prescribed disease under the Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit scheme. Record the occupational history now; raise it only if relevant.

professional.t: He may still decline. Explain the specific risks of not investigating, check he understands, record his decision and keep the offer open (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).
Track the MSU, FBC and referral to completion; a suspected cancer referral needs a practice system to confirm the appointment happens.

community.t: Cruse Bereavement Support; Fight Bladder Cancer and Macmillan for information if needed; Prostate Cancer UK for balanced PSA information.

redFlags: Visible haematuria at any point — NICE NG12 criteria for 45 and over
Dysuria or raised white cell count with non-visible haematuria at 60 and over — suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12)
Weight loss, loin pain, fever or urinary retention
psychosocial: Recently widowed and letting his health slide
Dread of hospitals and specifically of cystoscopy
Fear of facing bad news alone
ice: Idea: if he can’t see blood, it can’t be significant
Concern: a “camera up there”; bad news with no one to share it
Expectation: leave it and recheck later

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest: “Your urine has had blood in it twice that you can’t see. Often there’s a harmless cause, but at 67 with your smoking and your old job, it needs proper checking — invisible doesn’t mean harmless.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s like a warning light on a car dashboard. The car still drives fine and you can’t see anything wrong, but the light means a mechanic should have a look. Most of the time it’s something small — but you don’t ignore the light.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been through so much since your wife died, and the thought of tests with bad news at the end, on your own, is a lot. You won’t be on your own — I’ll be with you at each step.”
management.psychosocial: Build continuity into the plan: the same GP phones with results, written information about cystoscopy, and an offer of bereavement support.
sharedPlan: MSU, FBC, U&E/eGFR, urine ACR, BP; PSA and DRE after counselling (LUTS)
Urology referral: suspected cancer pathway if dysuria or raised white cell count (NICE NG12); otherwise routine urology for persistent non-visible haematuria at 40 and over
Nephrology if ACR 30 or more with haematuria (NICE NG203)
safetyNet: Same-day contact for visible blood, retention, fever or loin pain
GP tracks results and referral; phone follow-up with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candidates lose this station by accepting his logic that invisible means harmless, by quoting the wrong NICE NG12 threshold, or by pushing tests on a grieving man without finding out why he is reluctant.

items.fail: Agreeing to recheck the urine in three months.
items.why: Persistent non-visible haematuria is already confirmed; delay in a high-risk man is unsafe management.
items.fix: “It’s been confirmed twice. At your age and with your history, we check it properly now.”

items.fail: Quoting the visible haematuria criterion, or referring urgently without checking the white cell count.
items.why: NICE NG12 for non-visible haematuria requires age 60 and over plus dysuria or a raised white cell count. Precision is marked.
items.fix: Ask about dysuria and send an FBC; route the referral by the result.

items.fail: Never asking about occupation or smoking.
items.why: Aromatic amine exposure and 35 pack-years are central to his risk and to persuading him.
items.fix: Ask about past work and smoking and explain why they matter.

items.fail: Pressing on with the plan when he says “I’ve had enough of hospitals lately”.
items.why: “Does not respond to cues.” The bereavement is why he is avoiding tests.
items.fix: Reflect it back — “Lately?” — and give him space.

items.fail: Telling him cystoscopy is nothing to worry about.
items.why: Dismissing a specific fear rarely removes it.
items.fix: Describe it concretely and offer written information.

items.fail: Promising he will be seen within two weeks.
items.why: The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard is a diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days; a two-week promise is outdated.
items.fix: “On the urgent route, the aim is an answer within four weeks.”
